before: Sometimes it's the exercise that works. You feel real care for your little one and say exactly what they needed to hear. And a few days later you're skipping lunch and saying yes to everything again. A lot of people's first guess is that they didn't go deep enough. I don't think that's it, though, and I don't think this one failed either. Maybe the grown-up just hasn't come out of the exercise with you yet. Whatever you did for your little one in there, I'd try a tiny bit of it out here, like texting a friend that you're having a rough day instead of saying you're fine. That can honestly be harder than the meditation was. One small thing like that can teach your little one more than ten more good meditations. It doesn't have to happen after every session, and once isn't proof you've got it all down.

guide_passage:
The r4 guide's passage (the passage this carries): the whole h3 "When the Urge to Escape Arrives"
Sometimes the protective response is a sudden desire for a substance, a relationship, a new project, or anything else that can move attention away from pain. Don’t shame the urge. Notice what it may be signaling: something painful has come close enough to require management. That can be progress.

Thank the protective part. Slow down. Bring in support when the material is bigger than your present capacity.

This is also why I caution against forcing your way into intensive meditation, plant medicine, or aggressive trauma processing before enough Nurturer and Protector capacity exists. Those tools can break through protective layers faster than you can build the ability to hold what comes through.

Your own track record with psychoactive substances matters. One episode of voices, paranoia, major loss of reality testing, or a perceptual disturbance that persists beyond the expected intoxication is already enough reason not to retest that substance without professional assessment, even if you later feel stable. Treat that history as a vulnerability that also matters when considering other psychoactive substances that can disturb reality testing, without turning it into a claim that every drug is dangerous for you. Repeated milder confusion or dissociation matters too. Get prompt professional help when symptoms are severe, risky, or make safety uncertain, and especially when they persist or recur while sober. Do not abruptly stop a prescribed medicine or any substance you are physically dependent on just because it may be contributing; get appropriate medical guidance for stopping safely.

Listening to the guards is part of the therapy.

Gentle meditation or self-hypnosis can still help. My warning is about intensive versions. Gentle versions can genuinely help to calm the nervous system. Many people find that if there’s a mantra that they feel some heart connection to, repeating that mentally or verbally, especially with a nice melody, can lower the defense walls enough to allow the heart to open up. It’s not something to do all the time as a continuous cope, but it can be super effective when used therapeutically. I personally love this beautiful Om Mane Pemme Hum mantra that I found in the Garchen Rinpoche documentary, For the Benefit of All Beings:

[the YouTube video: Garchen Rinpoche, Om Mane Pemme Hum, from the documentary For the Benefit of All Beings]
